transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

I came in because I just can’t get my mind to let go of these awful thoughts that I’ve missed something important. Like, I work with numbers, so I’ll think, what if there was a wrong number in a data release, and then it spirals—though it’s not just work, it can be the back door, or a bill coming from the wrong account, little things that shouldn’t feel little.

I’ll know I checked it, or at least I think I know, but then my brain says, “What if you didn’t?” And then it feels like if I ignore that thought, I could cause some huge disaster. It sounds dramatic when I say it out loud. My daughter says I over-explain things—she’s probably right, I do that with grocery lists too—but the main thing is these thoughts just won’t leave me alone.
Do you feel the need to do something, like check or repeat an action, to make these thoughts go away?

Yes… I do. I mean, I tell myself I’m just being careful, because in my line of work one little number can make everything look wrong, you know? But it turns into this whole thing.

I’ll reopen the spreadsheet after I’ve already closed it, then reread the email line by line, sometimes more than once, and I have to check things in a certain order or it doesn’t feel… safe, I guess. Same at home with the locks, or with payment confirmations—like did the bill come out of the right account, did I click the right thing.

And then I lose time. I’ll think it’ll take five minutes, and suddenly it’s hours later, I’m still at my desk, and somehow nothing feels actually finished.
Do you feel anxious when you're unable to perform these checking or repeating behaviors?

Yes, very anxious. It’s like my chest tightens until I go back and do it “properly,” even if I was already done.

So I’ll reopen the spreadsheet, reread the email line by line, check the lock again, check the payment confirmation again—always in this order I’ve made up, which sounds silly, but if I don’t do it that way it doesn’t feel safe. My daughter says I make everything into a procedure, even packing leftovers, and she’s not wrong, but with this it’s not funny.

I’ll tell myself, just one more check so I can calm down, and then some nights I’m still sitting at my desk hours later, and nothing feels actually finished.
Do you ever avoid certain situations or tasks because of these thoughts or the need to check and repeat actions?

Yes… I do avoid things now, or I guess I end up missing them because I can’t get out the door, or away from my computer.

At work, I’ve fallen behind on major deadlines because I stay late reviewing things over and over, and somehow I still don’t feel done. Which is ridiculous, because the whole point of staying late is to finish, right? I used to be the person who had things turned in neatly, with the little color-coded notes—my daughter teases me about that, she says I make office supplies into a personality.

And outside work, I’ve stopped going to salsa nights, and I haven’t been kayaking either. I’ll think, “I’ll just check this one thing first,” and then it’s too late, or I’m too wound up to go. Salsa used to be fun, even though I’m not as coordinated as I like to pretend. But now I just… don’t make it there.
Do you experience any physical symptoms like palpitations, sweating, or trembling when you're feeling anxious about not checking or repeating these actions?

I’m not sure, honestly. I don’t always pay attention to my body in that moment because I’m so focused on whether I checked the thing the “right” way.

I mean, I know I feel worked up, but whether it’s palpitations or sweating or trembling… I don’t know. I might notice my hands feel a little off, but then I get distracted thinking, well, did I actually verify the formula cell or did I just look at it? And then I’m back in the spreadsheet.

Sorry, I know that’s not a very clean answer. I just haven’t really tracked those physical symptoms.
Do you have thoughts that aren't about checking or repeating actions, but still feel intrusive or unwanted?

Yes… I mean, the checking is what I end up doing, but the thought itself is the problem. It’s this awful, unwanted idea that I’ve missed something critical—like a wrong number in a data release, or the back door being unlocked, or a bill coming out of the wrong account.

And even if I know I checked it, my mind keeps saying, “But what if you didn’t? What if this causes some huge disaster?” It just won’t let go. I’ll be trying to move on to something else—sometimes something completely normal, like making coffee, or thinking about what my daughter said about needing better dish towels, which I know is not the point—and then the thought pops back in like it’s urgent.

So yes, they’re intrusive. I don’t want them. I’m not sitting there trying to worry about spreadsheets or bills for fun. It just grabs onto the possibility that I caused something terrible by missing one detail.
Do you feel like these intrusive thoughts are a part of who you are, or do they feel like they're coming from outside of yourself?

They feel like they’re coming from me, I guess—not like a voice outside my head or anything—but they don’t feel like me, if that makes sense.

I came in because I keep getting these awful, unwanted thoughts that I’ve missed something critical, like a wrong number in a data release, or the back door being unlocked, or a bill coming out of the wrong account. And even when I know I checked it, my mind just won’t let go of the possibility that I’ve caused some disaster.

It’s strange because I’m usually a careful person—sometimes too careful, my daughter would definitely say too careful—but these thoughts feel intrusive, like they barge in and take over. Not like my values or what I want to be thinking about.
Do you often worry about everyday things, like finances, relationships, or health, even when there's no apparent reason to worry?

I’m not sure how to separate that out, honestly. I mean, everyone worries about finances and health, right? Especially now, everything costs more, and then you get some random envelope in the mail and think, what is this going to be?

But I don’t know if I worry for no reason in a general way. My mind tends to latch onto something specific, and then I go down that path. Like, if I’m paying a bill, I’ll start thinking about whether I used the right account, and then somehow I’m also thinking about how we really need to replace the dish towels because my daughter made a comment about them—sorry, that’s not really what you asked.

So… I guess I can’t say clearly. I haven’t really noticed it as just everyday worrying without a reason. It’s more that once something catches my attention, I have trouble letting it go.
Do you feel like these thoughts are in line with your own values and beliefs, or do they feel like they're contradicting them?

No, they don’t feel in line with me. I mean… I’m a careful person, I work with numbers, I take that seriously. I don’t want to be the kind of person who misses some critical thing and causes a mess.

That’s why it’s so upsetting, I think. The thought is like, what if I put a wrong number in a data release, or what if the back door is unlocked, or what if I paid a bill from the wrong account—and even after I’ve checked, it keeps insisting there’s some disaster I caused.

It feels against what I believe about myself, I guess. Like my brain is accusing me of being careless when I’m trying so hard not to be. And then I’ll be standing there thinking about something completely different, like whether I bought the right coffee filters, and it comes right back. So no… it doesn’t feel like me.
Do you feel anxious or on edge most of the time, even when you're not thinking about these specific worries?

I don’t know if I’d say most of the time. I mean, I can be tense, but then I wonder if that’s just being a person with responsibilities, you know? Work, bills, the house… and my daughter will tell me I’m always “keyed up,” but she also says that when I’m just trying to get us out the door on time.

When I’m not thinking about one of those specific things, I don’t always notice it. Sometimes I’ll realize my shoulders are up by my ears, but then I’m thinking about whether I remembered to move the laundry, or what we’re having for dinner, and—sorry, I’m drifting.

So I guess I’m not sure. I haven’t really paid attention to whether I’m anxious when there isn’t a particular worry attached to it.
Do you generally feel anxious or uneasy even when you're not thinking about these specific worries or checking behaviors?

I’m not really sure. I think I’d have to catch myself at a moment when I’m not already focused on something, and that’s hard to tell.

Like, I can be sitting at the kitchen table and feel sort of uneasy, but then I’m also looking at the stack of mail, or remembering I forgot to call the dentist, or thinking my daughter left her shoes in the hallway again—sorry, that’s not exactly the question.

So… generally? I don’t know. I haven’t noticed it as a separate feeling, apart from whatever I’m already thinking about.
Do you feel anxious when you're not thinking about these specific worries or checking behaviors?

I honestly don’t know. I keep trying to separate it out, like “am I anxious for no reason right now,” but then there’s always some reason nearby, if that makes sense.

Like even sitting here, I’m thinking about the question, but also whether I answered it correctly before, and then I think about something I need to do after this, and then it all kind of blends together. So I can’t really say yes or no clearly. I haven’t noticed it as its own thing, apart from whatever I’m already caught up in.
Do you feel anxious when you are not thinking about any specific problems or worries?

I’m still not sure how to tell. If there’s absolutely no specific problem in my head… I mean, that’s rare, because there’s usually something floating around, even something small, like whether I left a light on or if I need to pick up groceries—sorry.

I don’t know that I’ve noticed anxiety just sitting there by itself. It’s more like I notice it after I’ve already attached it to something. So I can’t really give you a clean yes or no.
Do you feel anxious when you are completely relaxed and not thinking about anything in particular?

Completely relaxed… I’m not sure I really know what that means for me. I mean, if I’m sitting with tea or something, I’ll think, okay, this is supposed to be relaxing, but then I’m noticing the mug has a ring under it, or I remember something I meant to write down, or—I’m getting off track.

I don’t think I’ve noticed being anxious when there’s truly nothing in my mind. I’m not sure I ever catch that moment clearly enough to answer it.
Do you feel anxious when you are in a situation where none of your specific worries are present?

I don’t know. I’m trying to think of a situation where none of them are present, but then once I start looking for one, I sort of create one, if that makes sense.

Like if I’m at the grocery store, that should just be normal, but then I’m thinking about whether I picked the right line, or whether I forgot something, or—actually the grocery store is a bad example because there’s always something there. Maybe watching television, but even then I’ll notice something else.

So… I haven’t really noticed anxiety in a totally clear, worry-free situation. I’m not sure I can separate it that neatly.
Do you feel like you're generally a worrier, even when there aren't any specific problems or concerns in your life?

I’m not sure I’d call myself a worrier in that general way. I mean, my sister would probably say I am, but she says that about everyone, and she’s always been the dramatic one—well, not dramatic, just very sure of herself.

I think if there’s nothing specific going on, I don’t really know what my mind would do. Usually there’s some little thing to latch onto, even if it’s not important. But if you mean just worrying for no reason at all, I don’t know that I can say yes. I haven’t really noticed it that cleanly.
Do you often find yourself worrying about everyday things, like finances or relationships, even when everything seems to be going well?

I’m not sure. Everyday things, yes, but “finances or relationships” makes it sound more organized than it feels. Like bills—I mean, I pay them, or I try to keep track, but then I’ll remember I needed to check something else entirely, like whether I left a note in the wrong notebook. I have too many notebooks, honestly.

When things are going well… I don’t know if I stop and think, “everything is going well.” I’m usually just moving on to the next little thing. So I can’t really say I often worry about those kinds of things for no reason. I’d need to think about what you mean by “going well.”
Do you think your anxiety would still be present even if you didn't have these specific thoughts about checking and repeating actions?

I don’t think it would, or… not in the same way. The reason I came in is because my mind keeps grabbing onto these awful possibilities, like I missed something critical. A wrong number in a data release, or the back door being unlocked, or a bill coming out of the wrong account.

And I know that sounds like normal checking, because everyone checks things—my coworker checks her calendar three times, but she says that’s just being organized. With me, even after I know I checked, it doesn’t settle. It’s like my mind won’t let go of the idea that I caused some disaster.

So if those thoughts weren’t there, I don’t know that the anxiety would just float around by itself. It feels tied to that possibility that I missed something important.

Do you think the anxiety you experience is primarily driven by these specific thoughts about checking and repeating actions, or is it more of a general feeling of worry that is not necessarily tied to those specific thoughts?

It feels mostly driven by those specific thoughts, yes. I mean, I can worry about ordinary things too, but this is different.

The reason I came in is that I keep getting these awful, unwanted thoughts that I’ve missed something critical—like a wrong number in a data release, or the back door being unlocked, or a bill coming out of the wrong account. And then even when I know I checked it, I don’t feel done with it. My mind keeps circling back like, “What if you caused something terrible?”

It’s not just a general worry floating around, I don’t think. It’s more like my brain grabs onto that one possibility and won’t let go.
Do you feel like your need to check and repeat actions is driven by a desire to control things?

I guess control is part of it, but it doesn’t feel like I’m trying to control the whole world or anything. It’s more like I’m trying to get that one thing to stop feeling dangerous.

Like with spreadsheets, I’ll reopen them and check the numbers again, then reread the email line by line, and then somehow I’m back checking the same confirmation or the lock or the payment thing. I do it in a certain order, because if I jump around it feels… not safe, I guess.

And then I’ll think I’m almost done, but I’m still sitting at my desk hours later, and nothing is actually finished. So yes, maybe it’s about control, but mostly it’s me trying to calm myself down.

target_item.reason: The question asks about anxiety when completely relaxed and not focused on any particular worry, which is not directly covered by the listed OCD symptom profiles of obsessions, compulsions, or functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Completely relaxed… I’m not sure I really know what that means for me. I mean, if I’m sitting with tea or something, I’ll think, okay, this is supposed to be relaxing, but then I’m noticing the mug has a ring under it, or I remember something I meant to write down, or—I’m getting off track.

I don’t think I’ve noticed being anxious when there’s truly nothing in my mind. I’m not sure I ever catch that moment clearly enough to answer it.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's anxiety is generalized or specific to their obsessive thoughts
doctor.question: Do you feel anxious when you are in a situation where none of your specific worries are present?

target_item.reason: The question asks about anxiety occurring when no specific worries are present, which is not directly covered by the provided OCD symptom profiles focused on obsessions, compulsions, and functional impairment.

patient.answer:
I don’t know. I’m trying to think of a situation where none of them are present, but then once I start looking for one, I sort of create one, if that makes sense.

Like if I’m at the grocery store, that should just be normal, but then I’m thinking about whether I picked the right line, or whether I forgot something, or—actually the grocery store is a bad example because there’s always something there. Maybe watching television, but even then I’ll notice something else.

So… I haven’t really noticed anxiety in a totally clear, worry-free situation. I’m not sure I can separate it that neatly.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's anxiety is generalized and not limited to specific worries or checking behaviors
doctor.question: Do you feel like you're generally a worrier, even when there aren't any specific problems or concerns in your life?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about being a general worrier or having anxiety even without specific concerns, which is more about generalized/free-floating worry than the listed OCD symptoms of intrusive obsessions, compulsive checking, or functional impairment.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure I’d call myself a worrier in that general way. I mean, my sister would probably say I am, but she says that about everyone, and she’s always been the dramatic one—well, not dramatic, just very sure of herself.

I think if there’s nothing specific going on, I don’t really know what my mind would do. Usually there’s some little thing to latch onto, even if it’s not important. But if you mean just worrying for no reason at all, I don’t know that I can say yes. I haven’t really noticed it that cleanly.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of excessive worry about everyday things
doctor.question: Do you often find yourself worrying about everyday things, like finances or relationships, even when everything seems to be going well?

target_item.reason: The question is about generalized worry over everyday life areas like finances or relationships even when things are going well, which is not specifically covered by the OCD symptom profile items focused on intrusive obsessions, checking compulsions, or functional impairment.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure. Everyday things, yes, but “finances or relationships” makes it sound more organized than it feels. Like bills—I mean, I pay them, or I try to keep track, but then I’ll remember I needed to check something else entirely, like whether I left a note in the wrong notebook. I have too many notebooks, honestly.

When things are going well… I don’t know if I stop and think, “everything is going well.” I’m usually just moving on to the next little thing. So I can’t really say I often worry about those kinds of things for no reason. I’d need to think about what you mean by “going well.”

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's anxiety is better explained by a broader generalized anxiety pattern or specific obsessive-compulsive symptoms
doctor.question: Do you think your anxiety would still be present even if you didn't have these specific thoughts about checking and repeating actions?

target_item.name: Obsessions
target_item.manifestation: I came in because I keep getting these awful, unwanted thoughts that I’ve missed something critical—a wrong number in a data release, an unlocked back door, a bill paid from the wrong account—and even when I know I checked it, my mind won’t let go of the possibility that I’ve caused a disaster.
target_item.reason: The question is asking whether the anxiety is tied to the specific intrusive worries and thoughts about needing to check or repeat things, which most directly matches obsessions.

patient.answer:
I don’t think it would, or… not in the same way. The reason I came in is because my mind keeps grabbing onto these awful possibilities, like I missed something critical. A wrong number in a data release, or the back door being unlocked, or a bill coming out of the wrong account.

And I know that sounds like normal checking, because everyone checks things—my coworker checks her calendar three times, but she says that’s just being organized. With me, even after I know I checked, it doesn’t settle. It’s like my mind won’t let go of the idea that I caused some disaster.

So if those thoughts weren’t there, I don’t know that the anxiety would just float around by itself. It feels tied to that possibility that I missed something important.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's anxiety is better explained by obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) or generalized anxiety disorder (GAD)
doctor.question: Do you think the anxiety you experience is primarily driven by these specific thoughts about checking and repeating actions, or is it more of a general feeling of worry that is not necessarily tied to those specific thoughts?

target_item.name: Obsessions
target_item.manifestation: I came in because I keep getting these awful, unwanted thoughts that I’ve missed something critical—a wrong number in a data release, an unlocked back door, a bill paid from the wrong account—and even when I know I checked it, my mind won’t let go of the possibility that I’ve caused a disaster.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the anxiety is driven by the specific intrusive thoughts about missed errors or disasters rather than general worry, which directly matches obsessions.

patient.answer:
It feels mostly driven by those specific thoughts, yes. I mean, I can worry about ordinary things too, but this is different.

The reason I came in is that I keep getting these awful, unwanted thoughts that I’ve missed something critical—like a wrong number in a data release, or the back door being unlocked, or a bill coming out of the wrong account. And then even when I know I checked it, I don’t feel done with it. My mind keeps circling back like, “What if you caused something terrible?”

It’s not just a general worry floating around, I don’t think. It’s more like my brain grabs onto that one possibility and won’t let go.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's anxiety is primarily driven by the need for control
doctor.question: Do you feel like your need to check and repeat actions is driven by a desire to control things?

target_item.name: Compulsions
target_item.manifestation: To calm myself down I end up reopening spreadsheets, rereading emails line by line, checking locks and payment confirmations over and over in a set order until it feels 'safe,' and some nights I’m still at my desk hours later with nothing actually finished.
target_item.reason: The question is directly about the need to check and repeat actions, which corresponds to compulsive behaviors performed to reduce distress from the obsessive thoughts.

patient.answer:
I guess control is part of it, but it doesn’t feel like I’m trying to control the whole world or anything. It’s more like I’m trying to get that one thing to stop feeling dangerous.

Like with spreadsheets, I’ll reopen them and check the numbers again, then reread the email line by line, and then somehow I’m back checking the same confirmation or the lock or the payment thing. I do it in a certain order, because if I jump around it feels… not safe, I guess.

And then I’ll think I’m almost done, but I’m still sitting at my desk hours later, and nothing is actually finished. So yes, maybe it’s about control, but mostly it’s me trying to calm myself down.
